content: The Southeast Asia Tobacco Control Alliance (SEATCA) published the 2019 Southeast Asia Tobacco Industry Interference Index, a collaborative effort with the World Health Organization (WHO) South-East Asia Regional Office (SEARO). This report was made possible through the contributions of country collaborators who prepared detailed reports and reviewed evidence. The Index aims to highlight the extent of tobacco industry interference in public health policies across Southeast Asia and to encourage action to counter such interference. The Index acknowledges the invaluable input of collaborators from various countries, including Bangladesh (Knowledge for Progress PROGGA), India (Health Related Information Dissemination Amongst Youth HRIDAY), Indonesia (Indonesian Public Health Association IPHA), Maldives (Maldives NCD Alliance), Myanmar (People’s Health Foundation PHF), Nepal (Health Rights and Tobacco Control District Network RECPHEC), Sri Lanka (Alcohol and Drug Information Centre ADIC), Thailand (Action on Smoking or Health ASH Thailand), and Timor-Leste (NCD Alliance). Special thanks are extended to Dr. Thaksaphon Thamarangsi and Dr. Jagdish Kaur from WHO SEARO for their support. The Index builds upon its predecessor, the Asian Tobacco Industry Interference Index, and aims to generate discussions and drive actions to mitigate tobacco industry interference, which undermines tobacco control efforts. Key Findings: 1. Low Interference and Strong Tobacco Control: The government does not accept recommendations, collaborate on policy development, or endorse corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities from the tobacco industry. The Ministry of Health enforces strict rules to limit interactions with the industry. 2. Challenges in Response to Interference: Nepal has faced significant challenges from the tobacco industry, including legal battles over packaging laws. Despite this, the government has limited its interactions with the industry and does not accept its recommendations. Timor-Leste, one of the poorest countries globally, has shown political will by adopting the world’s largest pictorial health warnings on cigarette packs, despite high smoking prevalence among men. 3. Bangladesh and Indonesia exhibit weaker responses to tobacco industry interference. In Bangladesh, unnecessary interactions, such as awarding the tobacco industry for being a top taxpayer, open doors for lobbying against tobacco control policies. 4. Exclusion of Tobacco Industry from International Negotiations: None of the countries in the region included tobacco industry representatives in their delegations to FCTC-related meetings, such as the Conference of the Parties (COP). 5. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Activities: Tobacco-related CSR activities remain a significant issue in most countries, except for Maldives and Timor-Leste. These activities often target vulnerable communities and gain attention from high-level government officials, making it difficult for governments to reject them. 6. Benefits to the Tobacco Industry: Delayed legislation, tax exemptions, and subsidies continue to benefit the tobacco industry in several countries. For example, Nepal has not enforced penalties for non-compliance with packaging laws, and Indonesia allows cigarette advertisements on television. 7. Transparency and Conflict of Interest: Transparency in interactions with the tobacco industry remains a challenge across the region. Most countries lack procedures for disclosing meetings with the industry or maintaining records of such interactions. Additionally, conflicts of interest arise when senior government officials hold positions in tobacco companies or join the industry after retirement. Recommendations: To strengthen tobacco control policies and reduce industry interference, governments should: Ban tobacco-related CSR activities and other forms of contributions from the industry. Improve transparency by limiting interactions with the tobacco industry to only those strictly necessary for regulation and disclosing all records of such interactions. Adopt a code of conduct to guide government officials in dealing with the tobacco industry. Require tobacco companies to periodically submit detailed information on their business activities, including production, marketing expenditures, and lobbying efforts. The Index underscores the need for governments to take immediate and decisive actions to protect public health policies from tobacco industry interference.
